questions.q: A circular coil of radius 5 cm has 100 turns and is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. What is the magnetic flux linked with the coil? State the SI unit of magnetic flux.
questions.a: Magnetic flux Φ = NBA cosθ = 100 × 0.2 T × π(0.05 m)² × cos0° = 100 × 0.2 × π × 0.0025 = 0.157 Wb. SI unit: weber (Wb) = T·m². A wrong answer (e.g., forgetting N, using diameter instead of radius, or omitting cosθ) reveals the student confuses flux through one turn vs total flux linkage, or misapplies the area formula.

questions.q: In Faraday's Experiment 6.3 (two stationary coils, one connected to battery via tapping key), the galvanometer shows a momentary deflection when the key is pressed and released, but zero deflection when held pressed. Explain WHY this happens using the concept of magnetic flux and its rate of change.
questions.a: When key is pressed, current in coil C2 rises from 0 to maximum → magnetic field builds up → flux through coil C1 *changes* (dΦ/dt ≠ 0) → emf induced. When key held pressed, current is constant → magnetic field constant → flux constant (dΦ/dt = 0) → no emf. When key released, current falls to 0 → flux decreases (dΦ/dt ≠ 0) → emf induced in opposite direction. A wrong answer (e.g., "current in C2 induces current in C1 directly") reveals the student thinks steady current induces emf, missing the crucial role of *changing* flux.

questions.q: A square loop of side 20 cm and resistance 2 Ω is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The field is reduced to zero uniformly in 0.4 s. Calculate the magnitude of induced emf and the induced current in the loop.
questions.a:
Given: side = 0.2 m → A = 0.04 m²; B_initial = 0.5 T, B_final = 0; Δt = 0.4 s; N = 1; θ = 0°.
Initial flux Φ_i = BA = 0.5 × 0.04 = 0.02 Wb. Final flux Φ_f = 0.
|ΔΦ| = 0.02 Wb. |ε| = |ΔΦ/Δt| = 0.02 / 0.4 = 0.05 V = 50 mV.
Induced current I = |ε|/R = 0.05 / 2 = 0.025 A = 25 mA.
A wrong answer (e.g., using B instead of ΔB, forgetting area, or wrong Δt) reveals unit confusion (Wb vs T) or misunderstanding that emf depends on *rate of change* of flux, not flux itself.

questions.q: Two identical coils A and B are placed coaxially. Coil A carries a steady current I. Coil B is moved slowly towards coil A. Compare the induced emf in coil B when: (i) it is moved with constant velocity v, (ii) it is moved with constant acceleration a. Explain the physical reason for the difference.
questions.a: (i) Constant v → flux through B increases at constant rate (dΦ/dt = constant) → induced emf is constant. (ii) Constant a → velocity increases → rate of flux change increases (dΦ/dt increases) → induced emf increases with time. The difference arises because emf depends on *rate of change* of flux, which is proportional to relative velocity. A wrong answer (e.g., "emf is same in both cases") reveals the student thinks emf depends only on flux magnitude, not its time derivative.

questions.q: A student solves Example 6.2 from NCERT but writes: "Initial flux = BA = 0.1 × 0.01 = 0.001 Wb" (using side 10 cm = 0.1 m, area = 0.01 m², but forgetting cos45°). They get ε = 1.43 mV instead of 1.0 mV. Identify the error and explain why the angle between area vector and magnetic field matters.
questions.a: The student used θ = 0° (cosθ = 1) but the problem states the field is in the north-east direction while the loop is in the east-west plane → angle between area vector (normal to plane) and B is 45°. Correct flux = BA cos45° = 0.1 × 0.01 × 1/√2 = 7.07×10⁻⁴ Wb. The error shows the student treats flux as scalar BA instead of dot product B·A. Flux depends on the *component* of B normal to the surface; only the perpendicular component contributes.

questions.q: Design a simple classroom experiment to demonstrate that induced emf depends on the *rate* of change of magnetic flux, not just the total change. Specify materials, procedure, and what observations would confirm Faraday's law.
questions.a: Materials: Strong bar magnet, coil (50+ turns), galvanometer (or LED + resistor), stopwatch. Procedure: (1) Move magnet toward coil slowly (2 s) — note max deflection. (2) Move same magnet same distance quickly (0.5 s) — note larger max deflection. (3) Move magnet same speed but use coil with more turns — note larger deflection. Observations: Faster motion → larger emf (dΦ/dt larger); more turns → larger emf (N times). This confirms ε ∝ N|dΦ/dt|. A poor answer (e.g., "use stronger magnet") tests flux magnitude, not rate of change.
